# scplotter to work with NanoString CosMx data prepared by Giotto — human pancreas[¶](#scplotter-to-work-with-NanoString-CosMx-data-prepared-by-Giotto-%E2%80%94-human-pancreas)

# scplotter to work with NanoString CosMx data prepared by Giotto — human pancreas[¶](#scplotter-to-work-with-NanoString-CosMx-data-prepared-by-Giotto-%E2%80%94-human-pancreas)

**The technology.** CosMx SMI (NanoString) is an imaging-based,
subcellular platform: a targeted RNA panel is detected in situ and every
transcript keeps its own x/y coordinate, alongside cell and subcellular
segmentation from morphology images. A single field of view covers only
a small area, so one tissue is acquired as many FOVs that Giotto
composites into a single coordinate space.

**What this notebook covers.** The human pancreas FFPE dataset, exported
in the *current* flat-file format. Unlike the legacy export in the
companion notebook `Giotto.Nanostring_CosMx.ipynb`, this one ships a
pre-aggregated cell-by-feature matrix, so the object can be built with
`load_expression = TRUE` and no transcript-overlap step is needed. From
there: filtering, log normalisation, PCA/UMAP, Leiden clustering, and
the scplotter views (`CellStatPlot`, `SpatDimPlot`, `SpatFeaturePlot`)
on markers of the major pancreatic compartments.

Two things to watch that differ from the legacy workflow:
`version = "default"` selects the newer flat-file layout, and the
`SystemControl` feature type keeps the system-control probes out of the
RNA panel. The vendor also ships an InSituType cell-type call set
alongside the flat files; it is not used below but can be joined onto
the cell metadata if you want their labels.

**Data.** NanoString human pancreas FFPE, 18 FOVs — the dataset used in
the [Giotto CosMx pancreas
tutorial](https://giottosuite.com/articles/cosmx_pancreas.html).

**Before you run.** A Giotto Python environment (PCA/UMAP/Leiden call
into Python) and the pancreas bundle unpacked under `data/`. The
expression matrix is a multi-GB CSV, so give the kernel room.

In \[1\]:

    library(Giotto)

    # Record the stack this notebook was executed against.
    for (pkg in c("Giotto", "GiottoClass", "GiottoData", "GiottoVisuals", "GiottoUtils")) {
        cat(pkg, as.character(utils::packageVersion(pkg)), "\n")
    }

    # Ensure Giotto can access a python env
    genv_exists <- suppressMessages(checkGiottoEnvironment())
    print(genv_exists)

    python_path <- Sys.getenv("GIOTTO_PYTHON")
    Sys.setenv(RETICULATE_PYTHON = python_path)

    invisible(capture.output(suppressMessages(set_giotto_python_path(python_path = python_path))))

## The pancreas dataset[¶](#The-pancreas-dataset)

The Lung12 run above is a *legacy* export: Giotto aggregates subcellular
transcripts up to cell polygons itself, which is faithful but expensive.
Current CosMx exports also ship a pre-aggregated cell-by-feature matrix,
and when that exists it is much cheaper to start from — one file read
instead of overlapping millions of transcript coordinates.

This section uses the NanoString human pancreas FFPE dataset, the same
one used in the [Giotto CosMx pancreas
tutorial](https://giottosuite.com/articles/cosmx_pancreas.html). It
covers 18 FOVs. Two differences from Section 1 to watch:
`version = "default"` (newer flat-file layout) and the `SystemControl`
feature type, which keeps the system-control probes out of the RNA
panel. The vendor also ships an InSituType cell-type call set alongside
the flat files; it is not needed for the plots below but can be joined
onto the cell metadata if you want the vendor's labels.

In \[3\]:

    ## create a CosMx object from the pancreas export
    ## load_expression = TRUE reads the pre-aggregated exprMat file, so no transcript overlap step is
    ## needed; load_transcripts = FALSE keeps the multi-GB transcript table off the heap.
    pancreas_path <- "data/Pancreas-CosMx-WTx"

    pancreas <- suppressWarnings(createGiottoCosMxObject(
        cosmx_dir = pancreas_path,
        version = "default",
        load_expression = TRUE,
        load_transcripts = FALSE,
        feat_type = c("rna", "SystemControl"),
        split_keyword = list("SystemControl"),
        instructions = instrs
    ))

    force(pancreas)

### Filtering and normalisation[¶](#Filtering-and-normalisation)

Same minimum-count filtering as Section 1, then log normalisation and
per-cell statistics so the plotting functions have `total_expr` /
`nr_feats` to colour by.

In \[4\]:

    pancreas <- filterGiotto(pancreas,
        feat_type = "rna",
        expression_threshold = 1,
        feat_det_in_min_cells = 5,
        min_det_feats_per_cell = 5
    )

    pancreas <- normalizeGiotto(pancreas,
        feat_type = "rna",
        norm_methods = "standard"
    )

    pancreas <- addStatistics(pancreas,
        expression_values = "normalized",
        feat_type = "rna"
    )

    showGiottoCellMetadata(pancreas)

### Embedding and clustering[¶](#Embedding-and-clustering)

The pancreas export already carries a cell matrix, so the workflow is
the standard scRNA-seq one: PCA, UMAP, a nearest-neighbour graph, then
Leiden. Cluster labels come back as integers from the igraph
implementation, so they are converted to a factor here — otherwise the
plotting layer treats the cluster id as a continuous value and draws a
colour ramp instead of categories.

In \[5\]:

    ## Select highly variable features before PCA. runPCA()'s own default is feats_to_use = "hvf";
    ## passing NULL instead forces a PCA over every feature retained by filtering, and on this
    ## export that is ~19,000 features x ~48,000 cells, which does not finish in hours. calculateHVF()
    ## writes the "hvf" column that runPCA() then picks up, and is the standard Giotto workflow.
    pancreas <- calculateHVF(pancreas, expression_values = "normalized", HVFname = "hvf")
    pancreas <- runPCA(pancreas)
    pancreas <- runUMAP(pancreas, dimensions_to_use = seq(15), n_neighbors = 40)
    pancreas <- createNearestNetwork(pancreas, dimensions_to_use = seq(15), k = 40)
    pancreas <- doLeidenCluster(pancreas)

    # categorical, not numeric
    pancreas@cell_metadata$cell$rna$leiden_clus <-
        factor(pancreas@cell_metadata$cell$rna$leiden_clus)

     used to select highly variable features

### Plotting the pancreas section[¶](#Plotting-the-pancreas-section)

Cluster composition goes through scplotter's `CellStatPlot`. The spatial
views below call `SpatDimPlot()` / `SpatFeaturePlot()` on the object
with three settings this export needs: `spat_loc_name = "raw"` (where
its locations live), `crop = FALSE` (the images carry per-FOV local
extents while the cells sit in a global frame, so the default crop
removes every cell), and `points_x = "sdimx"` / `points_y = "sdimy"`
(scplotter does not set x/y for Giotto objects, and the metadata carries
a column named `X` -- the run id, constant 1 -- that would otherwise be
bound).

In \[6\]:

    options(repr.plot.width = 12, repr.plot.height = 6)

    p1 <- CellStatPlot(pancreas, ident = "leiden_clus")
    p2 <- CellStatPlot(pancreas, ident = "leiden_clus", plot_type = "pie")
    p1 + p2

In \[7\]:

    options(repr.plot.width = 7, repr.plot.height = 11)

    ## every cell in the composited frame, coloured by cluster
    SpatDimPlot(
        pancreas,
        group_by = "leiden_clus",
        feat_type = "rna",
        spat_loc_name = "raw",
        ## scplotter's points branch does not set x/y, and this export carries a metadata
        ## column named X (the CosMx run id, constant 1) that plotthis would otherwise bind.
        points_x = "sdimx",
        points_y = "sdimy",
        crop = FALSE
    )

In \[8\]:

    options(repr.plot.width = 12, repr.plot.height = 10)

    ## Keep only markers this panel detects in a useful number of cells: an undetected feature
    ## gives an empty facet, and the facetted plot then fails to build a viewport.
    fd <- fDataDT(pancreas)
    pancreas_markers <- intersect(c("INS", "GCG", "SST", "KRT19", "CPA1", "PRSS1"), fd$feat_ID)
    if ("nr_cells" %in% names(fd)) {
        pancreas_markers <- fd[feat_ID %in% pancreas_markers & nr_cells > 50, feat_ID]
    }
    cat("markers plotted:", paste(pancreas_markers, collapse = ", "), "\n")

    ## shapes = FALSE keeps this cheap: the export carries ~9.5 million cell polygons, and
    ## drawing them once per marker facet is what makes the plot run out of memory.
    SpatFeaturePlot(
        pancreas,
        features = pancreas_markers,
        feat_type = "rna",
        spat_loc_name = "raw",
        ## scplotter's points branch does not set x/y, and this export carries a metadata
        ## column named X (the CosMx run id, constant 1) that plotthis would otherwise bind.
        points_x = "sdimx",
        points_y = "sdimy",
        crop = FALSE,
        points = TRUE,
        shapes = FALSE
    )

    markers plotted: CPA1, GCG, INS, KRT19, PRSS1, SST

### Replicating the upstream vignette with scplotter[¶](#Replicating-the-upstream-vignette-with-scplotter)

Giotto Suite publishes a walkthrough for this dataset: [Whole
transcriptome CosMx Human Pancreas
FFPE](https://giottosuite.com/articles/cosmx_pancreas.html). The cells
below reproduce its figures **using scplotter**, so the analysis plots
here can be compared directly with the upstream ones.

Where each figure comes from:

- **Embeddings** (`CellDimPlot`) read the object's own reductions. The
  reduction names are stored lowercase (`pca`, `umap`, `tsne`), and
  `feat_type = "rna"` must be given explicitly because this object also
  carries a `SystemControl` feature type.
- **Spatial views** call `SpatDimPlot()` / `SpatFeaturePlot()` on the
  object, with `spat_loc_name = "raw"` (this export stores its locations
  under that name), `crop = FALSE` and explicit `points_x = "sdimx"` /
  `points_y = "sdimy"`. The crop is needed because the images carry
  per-FOV local extents while the cells sit in a global frame, and the
  explicit columns because scplotter does not set x/y for Giotto objects
  while this export has a metadata column named `X` (the run id,
  constant 1) that would otherwise be bound.
- **Marker expression in embedding space** uses
  `FeatureStatPlot(plot_type = "dim")`, which colours a reduction by
  feature values and facets one panel per feature.

Not reproduced: the subcellular figures (`spatInSituPlotPoints`, the
polygon-fill maps and the small-subset views). Those need the transcript
table, a 4.9 GB export; this notebook loads the pre-aggregated matrix
(`load_expression = TRUE`, `load_transcripts = FALSE`).

One honest difference: the vignette derives PCA from **pearson
residuals** (`calculateHVF(method = "var_p_resid")` on the `pearson`
matrix), while this notebook uses log-normalised values with
`calculateHVF()`'s default. The embeddings below are therefore this
notebook's, and the cluster numbering will not match the vignette's.

In \[9\]:

    options(repr.plot.width = 7, repr.plot.height = 11)

    ## Vignette section 10.2 - normalised total expression across the tissue
    SpatFeaturePlot(
        pancreas,
        features = "total_expr",
        feat_type = "rna",
        spat_loc_name = "raw",
        ## scplotter's points branch does not set x/y, and this export carries a metadata
        ## column named X (the CosMx run id, constant 1) that plotthis would otherwise bind.
        points_x = "sdimx",
        points_y = "sdimy",
        crop = FALSE,
        points = TRUE,
        shapes = FALSE
    )

In \[10\]:

    options(repr.plot.width = 10, repr.plot.height = 4)

    ## Vignette section 11.1 - cells in PCA space, coloured by number of detected features.
    ## nr_feats is continuous, and CellDimPlot's group_by is for factors, so this goes through
    ## FeatureStatPlot(plot_type = "dim").
    FeatureStatPlot(
        pancreas,
        features = "nr_feats",
        plot_type = "dim",
        reduction = "pca",
        feat_type = "rna"
    )

In \[11\]:

    ## Vignette section 11.2 - tSNE on the first ten PCs, as in the vignette.
    ## check_duplicates = FALSE: on a targeted panel many cells share identical PC coordinates, and
    ## Rtsne otherwise aborts with "Remove duplicates before running TSNE".
    pancreas <- runtSNE(pancreas, dimensions_to_use = 1:10, check_duplicates = FALSE)

    Setting dimension reduction [cell][rna] tsne

In \[12\]:

    options(repr.plot.width = 7, repr.plot.height = 6)

    ## Vignette section 11.2 - UMAP coloured by FOV: the two 3x3 imaging blocks separate cleanly
    CellDimPlot(pancreas, reduction = "umap", group_by = "fov", feat_type = "rna")

In \[14\]:

    options(repr.plot.width = 11, repr.plot.height = 7)

    ## Vignette section 11.3 - marker expression in UMAP space. FeatureStatPlot with
    ## plot_type = "dim" colours a reduction by feature values and facets one panel per feature.
    FeatureStatPlot(
        pancreas,
        features = c("COL1A1", "SPINK1", "GP2", "TTR"),
        plot_type = "dim",
        reduction = "umap",
        feat_type = "rna"
    )

In \[18\]:

    options(repr.plot.width = 7, repr.plot.height = 11)

    ## Vignette section 12.2 - clusters across the tissue, as points
    SpatDimPlot(
        pancreas,
        group_by = "leiden_clus",
        feat_type = "rna",
        spat_loc_name = "raw",
        ## scplotter's points branch does not set x/y, and this export carries a metadata
        ## column named X (the CosMx run id, constant 1) that plotthis would otherwise bind.
        points_x = "sdimx",
        points_y = "sdimy",
        crop = FALSE

In \[19\]:

    options(repr.plot.width = 7, repr.plot.height = 11)

    ## Vignette section 12.3 - the same clusters as filled cell polygons. The shape layer does not
    ## suffer the extent problem the points layer has, so it is drawn straight from the object.
    ## shapes_border_color = NA is required at this scale: the export has ~9.5 million polygons over
    ## 7 x 11 inches, so each cell is a fraction of a pixel and the per-polygon outline otherwise
    ## covers the fill, rendering the whole map black even though the fill is mapped correctly.
    SpatDimPlot(
        pancreas,
        group_by = "leiden_clus",
        feat_type = "rna",
        spat_loc_name = "raw",
        points = FALSE,
        shapes = TRUE,
        shapes_fill_by = "leiden_clus",
        shapes_border_color = NA
